answers.stem_only: AssumeRole itself fails although the caller's identity policy allows it, so the role's trust policy does not trust the development account (or its principals). Add the development account as a principal in the role's trust policy.

Cross-account access needs an allow on both sides: the role's identity-based policy in account A allows s3:GetObject on the bucket objects, and the bucket policy in account B allows s3:GetObject for that specific role ARN. No public principal, no IAM user keys.

The application already runs on EC2, so attach an IAM role through an instance profile to the existing instances; the SDK gets rotating temporary credentials from instance metadata. The private CA is irrelevant (Roles Anywhere is for workloads outside AWS).
An SCP that denies cloudtrail:StopLogging and cloudtrail:DeleteTrail (and similar), attached to the organization root so every current and future member account, including its root user, inherits it.
An explicit Deny overrides any Allow, from any policy, so adding allows cannot help. Remove the obsolete Deny statement from the customer managed policy.

Enable IAM Identity Center in the management account, use its built-in identity store as the identity source (no external IdP), create users and groups, and assign permission sets per group per account; employees use the single access portal sign-in for console and CLI.

Use a Cognito identity pool federated with the user pool to exchange the user's token for temporary credentials of an authenticated IAM role scoped to least privilege: s3:PutObject on the bucket (ideally per-user prefix).

The workload runs outside AWS and the company has a private CA, so use IAM Roles Anywhere: register the CA as a trust anchor, create a profile and role, and let the servers exchange their X.509 certificates for temporary role credentials.

An IAM group is not a principal and cannot be named in a resource-based policy. Name an actual principal: the individual IAM users' ARNs or an IAM role the analysts assume (or skip the bucket policy and grant access through the group's identity policy, since it is the same account).
Restrict iam:PassRole in the developers' policy to the ARNs of the two project roles (optionally with iam:PassedToService ec2.amazonaws.com), keeping ec2:RunInstances.
Bucket policy with Principal * and a condition aws:PrincipalOrgID equal to the organization ID, which automatically includes new accounts.

The key policy does not enable IAM policies (no statement for the account root), so the role's IAM allow for kms:Decrypt has no effect. Add a key policy statement that allows the application's role kms:Decrypt (or add the account-root statement to enable IAM policies).
Use IAM Access Analyzer policy generation, which reads the role's CloudTrail activity and generates a least-privilege policy template; review, refine, and replace AdministratorAccess.
Enable MFA on the root user, delete the root access key, stop using root for daily tasks; use IAM roles (Identity Center or federated roles for the founders, an instance profile role for the script).

For managed services such as S3 and DynamoDB, the customer is responsible for data, identity and access management (IAM permissions), and configuration; AWS owns the platform software, host OS and physical facilities.
IAM Identity Center with AD Connector as the identity source (a proxy, no second directory and no password copies in AWS), with permission sets assigned to AD groups across the 40 accounts.

Use a managed policy as a permissions boundary on each developer-created role (enforced by requiring iam:PermissionsBoundary on iam:CreateRole); the boundary caps the maximum while the role's own policy grants. SCPs would hit the other teams.

MFA-protected API access: require aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent true for s3:DeleteObject in the IAM policy, and have administrators call sts:GetSessionToken with their MFA code and use the returned temporary credentials for the CLI. Long-term access keys never carry MFA context; S3 MFA Delete is a root-only versioning feature.

Use the console's Revoke active sessions on the role, which attaches the AWSRevokeOlderSessions inline policy denying all actions when aws:TokenIssueTime is older than now; applications simply assume the role again.

Create a cross-account role trusting the vendor's AWS account with a read-only permissions policy, and require the vendor-generated unique sts:ExternalId in the trust policy condition to prevent the confused deputy problem.
IAM Access Analyzer external access analyzers are Regional, so create an organization-zone-of-trust analyzer (from the management or delegated admin account) in each of the three Regions used.

AssumeRole works, so trust is fine; the role session lacks S3 permission. Add s3:GetObject (bucket and objects) to the role's permissions policy; the bucket is in the same account so no bucket policy is needed.
